title: Raised intracranial pressure and herniation
subtitle: Recognise, buy time, decompress

sources.title: Guidelines for the management of severe traumatic brain injury, 4th edition (Carney et al, Neurosurgery 2017;80:6-15)

sources.org: Seattle International Severe Traumatic Brain Injury Consensus Conference (SIBICC)
sources.title: A management algorithm for patients with intracranial pressure monitoring (Hawryluk et al, Intensive Care Med 2019)
Trial of decompressive craniectomy for traumatic intracranial hypertension (Hutchinson et al, N Engl J Med 2016;375:1119-30)

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Head injury: assessment and early management (NG232)

red_flags.text: Falling GCS, particularly a fall in the motor score, in a patient with a known or suspected intracranial lesion.
A new unilateral dilated or sluggish pupil: uncal herniation compressing the third nerve until proven otherwise.
Extensor or flexor posturing, or a new hemiparesis.
Cushing response: hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing. This is a late, pre-terminal sign.
Monitored ICP above 22 mmHg that does not settle with first-tier measures.
Headache with vomiting and papilloedema, or a reduced conscious level, in a patient with a shunt, tumour or hydrocephalus.

do_now.text: Secure the airway. Intubate for GCS 8 or less or a falling GCS with signs of herniation, avoiding hypoxia and hypotension at induction.
Head up about 30 degrees, neck neutral, tube ties and collar not compressing the jugular veins.
For clinical signs of herniation, give a hyperosmolar agent (mannitol or hypertonic saline per local protocol) as a bridge to imaging and a neurosurgical decision.
Urgent CT head, and call neurosurgery at the same time, not after the report.

assess.text: GCS by component, pupils and limb movements, repeated and timed. The trend matters more than the single value.
Look for a cause that is treatable outside the skull: hypoxia, hypercapnia, hypotension, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, seizures and fever.
Ask about anticoagulants and antiplatelets, a shunt, a known tumour, recent surgery, and the time course of decline.
Estimate haematoma volume from the scan when a mass lesion is present.

investigate.text: CT head without contrast: mass lesion, midline shift, effacement of basal cisterns, hydrocephalus, and diffuse swelling.
Arterial blood gas, sodium, glucose, coagulation screen and full blood count.
Intracranial pressure monitoring in severe traumatic brain injury when the neurosurgical team judges it will guide treatment.
Repeat CT for any new deterioration or unexplained rise in ICP; a new surgical lesion must be excluded before escalating medical therapy.

resuscitate.text: Avoid hypotension. The BTF systolic thresholds are at least 100 mmHg at age 50 to 69, and at least 110 mmHg at age 15 to 49 or over 70.
Treat ICP above 22 mmHg, and target a cerebral perfusion pressure of 60 to 70 mmHg in severe traumatic brain injury.
Normal oxygenation and normocapnia. Do not use prolonged prophylactic hyperventilation; brief hyperventilation is only a bridge for active herniation.
Escalate in tiers: sedation and analgesia, CSF drainage if a ventricular drain is in place, hyperosmolar therapy, then higher-tier options agreed with neurosurgery and intensive care.
Do not give corticosteroids for traumatic brain injury; they increase mortality.
Consider early seizure prophylaxis in severe traumatic brain injury, per local protocol; it reduces early seizures but not late epilepsy.

definitive.text: Evacuate a surgical mass lesion (extradural, acute subdural, or contusion with mass effect) as an emergency.
External ventricular drainage for obstructive hydrocephalus or for ICP control when a drain is indicated.
Decompressive craniectomy as a last-tier option for refractory ICP: it reduces death, at the cost of more survivors with severe disability. Discuss this trade-off with the family.
If a craniectomy is performed, a large frontotemporoparietal flap is recommended over a small one.

escalate.text: Call neurosurgery at the first sign of herniation. Transfer is part of treatment, and hyperosmolar therapy only buys time for it.
Transfer intubated and ventilated with oxygenation and blood pressure controlled, images sent ahead, and a clinician who can manage the airway.
Involve intensive care early; tiered ICP management needs continuous monitoring and nursing that a ward cannot provide.

notes: A blown pupil is a sign of where the brain is going, not of what is wrong. The cure is usually a scan and an operation, not more mannitol.
Hyperventilation lowers ICP by making the brain ischaemic. Use it for minutes as a bridge, never as a strategy.
Before escalating any medical ICP therapy, ask whether something has changed that needs a new scan.
